sciencenews.org/article/atoms-gravity-sp.title: Free-falling atoms in space put a new twist on Galileo’s gravity test
sciencenews.org/article/atoms-gravity-sp.excerpt: Rubidium atoms on China’s Tiangong space station fell with the same acceleration, upholding a cornerstone of Einstein’s general theory of relativity.

phys.org/news/2026-08-plastic-welds-reta.title: How plastic welds retain a molecular 'memory' of their former surfaces to strengthen pipe joints
phys.org/news/2026-08-plastic-welds-reta.excerpt: Welding plastic is a critically important part of everyday engineering—especially for preventing leaks in underground water and gas pipes. For decades, engineers have understood that a properly welded joint in polyethylene pipe can be just as strong as the pipe itself, if not stronger. However, the reason for this strength has remained a mystery.

phys.org/news/2026-08-picture-eagle-migr.title: A never-before-seen picture of eagle migrations
phys.org/news/2026-08-picture-eagle-migr.excerpt: In 1899, scientists began tracking avian migration by placing a small ring with an identifier around birds' ankles. Researchers then had to recapture the birds elsewhere, leaving the journey between those points a mystery. Today, GPS tags allow researchers to see every stage of bird migration. The tags are small, have long-lasting batteries and solar panels, and track dozens of metrics. Migration is no longer described as just a theoretical range but rather as an exact map. Despite this technological advancement, the routes of many species in their respective flyways remain undescribed.

phys.org/news/2026-08-takeaway-cups-micr.title: Takeaway cups may be releasing microplastics into your coffee
phys.org/news/2026-08-takeaway-cups-micr.excerpt: Single-use paper cups used for takeout coffee and other beverages release millions of microplastic particles when exposed to hot liquid, University of Queensland researchers have found.

phys.org/news/2026-08-centuries-child-la.title: Centuries of child labor left lasting spinal damage in Dutch children, study finds
phys.org/news/2026-08-centuries-child-la.excerpt: Children in the postmedieval Dutch workforce worked so hard that their spines became worn and deformed, with some children affected before they even had a chance to lose their baby teeth, a new study published in the International Journal of Paleopathology finds.

phys.org/news/2026-08-children-consent-s.title: Talking to your children about consent and sexual violence can be hard. Here's how to start the conversation
phys.org/news/2026-08-children-consent-s.excerpt: There have been multiple high-profile alleged incidents of sexual violence against women and girls in news headlines this month. Some involve teenage boys.

phys.org/news/2026-08-nano-sandwich-phot.title: Nano-sandwich photocathode improves solar conversion of CO₂ into ethanol
phys.org/news/2026-08-nano-sandwich-phot.excerpt: Czech researchers at Charles University in Prague, led by Pavla Eliášová, have developed an advanced photocathode that helps convert the greenhouse gas carbon dioxide into pure ethanol using sunlight. The new technology solves a long-standing problem of material degradation in water, achieves record conversion efficiency and opens the way toward sustainable production of green fuels. The paper is published in the journal Advanced Energy Materials.

phys.org/news/2026-08-cities-urban-strea.title: Many cities buried urban streams. Here's how to bring them back
phys.org/news/2026-08-cities-urban-strea.excerpt: As many cities developed, streams that once flowed on the surface were buried underground to make way for growing infrastructure. However, as heavier rainfall, extreme weather and aging infrastructure place growing pressure on cities, these buried streams could become part of the solution.

phys.org/news/2026-08-rethinking-bluegre.title: Rethinking bluegreen aphid control as insecticide resistance spreads
phys.org/news/2026-08-rethinking-bluegre.excerpt: When an insecticide application fails to control bluegreen aphid, application conditions may not be the only cause. Research has identified resistant populations across southern Australia, confirming that repeated reliance on broad-spectrum insecticides is no longer sustainable.

phys.org/news/2026-08-aipowered-policing.title: How AI‑powered policing is endangering the public's trust in police
phys.org/news/2026-08-aipowered-policing.excerpt: Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, artificial intelligence (AI) has dominated the cultural landscape. Uptake across various sectors, including law enforcement, quickly followed, usually with minimal foresight and little to no guardrails, like effective policies or laws, to govern AI use.

phys.org/news/2026-08-climate-policy-peo.title: Climate policy could learn from people who already live within the limits of sufficiency
phys.org/news/2026-08-climate-policy-peo.excerpt: Tina Nyfors, who recently defended her doctoral thesis at the University of Helsinki, studied sufficiency, a way of living and a principle for organizing society to stay within environmental limits while ensuring that people have enough. Nyfors directs attention to people whose carbon footprint is already in line with sufficiency and refers to them as the sufficiency class. Their way of life has a moderate climate impact yet still meets their needs.

phys.org/news/2026-08-discovery-great-ba.title: The discovery of the Great Barrier Reef's whale maternity ward

phys.org/news/2026-08-galpagos-corals-el.title: Galápagos corals show El Niño events are more extreme now than in past 1,000 years
phys.org/news/2026-08-galpagos-corals-el.excerpt: Temperatures have warmed dramatically across the equatorial Pacific Ocean in 2026, signaling the onset of a strong and potentially historic El Niño. These events can affect weather around the world, and the intensity of recent El Niño events is raising alarm that, as global temperatures rise, they are becoming stronger and more destructive.

phys.org/news/2026-08-earlier-swathing-p.title: Earlier swathing opens a new pathway for subterranean clover seed harvest
phys.org/news/2026-08-earlier-swathing-p.excerpt: Subterranean clover's ability to bury its seed supports pasture persistence but makes commercial seed harvesting difficult. The industry relies on aging Horwood-Bagshaw (HB) suction harvesters, which collect seed from fully dry crops after repeated tillage and raking.

phys.org/news/2026-08-temperature-graphe.title: Low temperature graphene growth opens a route to sustainable resource recycling

Yet producing graphene typically requires temperatures as high as 900°C (1,652°F), limiting energy efficiency and making structural control difficult. To make graphene production more practical, a recent study has overcome this long-standing temperature barrier.

phys.org/news/2026-08-fast-fashion-carbo.excerpt: Fast fashion is built on cheap, short-lived garments, especially cotton and polyester T-shirts. To sustain its profits, the industry relies on high production frequency, short product lifespan and a globalized supply chain. All these elements contribute to making the industry a major source of global pollution.

phys.org/news/2026-08-scientists-capture.title: Scientists capture first molecular-level images of water reorganization during a reaction crucial for life

Honey bees continuously interact with their surrounding environment through the collection of nectar, pollen and water and can therefore be exposed to contaminants present in agricultural and natural ecosystems. Their health may consequently provide valuable information about environmental pressures affecting biodiversity and ecosystem functioning.

Researchers with the Dog Aging Project found that patterns of small molecules in dogs’ blood were linked to longer or shorter lifespans in remarkably similar ways to those seen in people. These metabolic “fingerprints” could offer clues about the biological processes that drive aging, including metabolism, inflammation, and cellular stress.

The discovery could eventually point toward new treatments designed to shift neurons from simply surviving an injury to actively rebuilding themselves.

universetoday.com/articles/spaceflight-l.title: Spaceflight Leaves Heart Muscle Cell Strength Intact
universetoday.com/articles/spaceflight-l.excerpt: Since the dawn of human space exploration, astronauts, scientists, and engineers have examined the short- and long-term effects of microgravity (often mistakenly called zero-gravity) on the human body. This includes the distribution of fluids to the upper body (called “puffy face”), an increase in height from the spine slightly extending, how solar and cosmic radiation impacts humans at the genetic level, and skeletal and muscle loss. However, arguably all these aspects pale in comparison to how the microgravity from spaceflight impacts the heart, and specifically heart muscle cells.

universetoday.com/articles/measuring-the.title: Measuring the Mass of the Universe Isn't As Simple as Astronomers Thought
universetoday.com/articles/measuring-the.excerpt: How do scientists know the mass of the Universe? Measuring it has traditionally relied on knowing how many stars there are in galaxies, as well as clouds of gas and dust, and associated dark matter. Astronomers generally use the mass of the brightest stars to estimate the mass of an entire galaxy. That means the rest of a galaxy's stars and its dark matter are essentially invisible. For decades, astronomers estimated the number of small, unseen stars in clusters and galaxies using a mathematical rule that assumed stars formed in roughly the same mass proportions everywhere in the Universe. That tool is called the initial mass function (IMF). It describes how many stars of each size there are in a given cluster or galaxy. However, there are challenges with the way it's currently applied because of assumptions it contains.

phys.org/news/2026-08-scientists-diamond.title: Scientists melted a diamond and cracked a secret of ice giants
phys.org/news/2026-08-scientists-diamond.excerpt: Some of the strangest weather in the solar system doesn't happen on Earth or even in Jupiter's Great Red Spot—it happens in the interiors of ice giants like Neptune and Uranus. Specifically, scientists have long believed that, at certain pressures and temperatures, it literally rains diamonds inside these planets. For the first time, scientists have mimicked the process they believe creates this phenomenon.

phys.org/news/2026-08-airborne-tuberculo.excerpt: Tuberculosis bacteria released into the air from infected individuals dry out to form infectious particles that are second only to measles in contagiousness. Weill Cornell Medicine investigators have discovered specific mechanisms that enable the bacteria not only to survive drying but also to generate mutations linked to antibiotic resistance. This suggests that transmission involves more than the passive movement of bacteria between people and may be a period during which the pathogen evolves.

molecular_water_reorganization.headline: Scientists Capture First Molecular‑Level Images of Water Reorganization in Proton‑Coupled Electron Transfer
molecular_water_reorganization.summary: Using ultrafast X‑ray spectroscopy and scattering, researchers visualized how water molecules rearrange as a proton‑electron transfer reaction proceeds, revealing unprecedented structural detail.
highlights: Ultrafast X‑ray methods at the Linac Coherent Light Source captured simultaneous electron and proton dynamics
Combined X‑ray absorption (chemRIXS) and scattering (XCS) revealed solvent reorganization around a ruthenium complex
Quantum chemistry and molecular dynamics simulations interpreted the transient X‑ray signals
Findings published in Nature Communications suggest pathways to more efficient catalysts and flow batteries

nano_sandwich_photocathode_co2_to_ethano.headline: Nano‑sandwich Photocathode Boosts Solar CO₂‑to‑Ethanol Conversion Efficiency
nano_sandwich_photocathode_co2_to_ethano.summary: A Charles University team created a Cu₂O‑MXene‑TiO₂ nano‑sandwich photocathode that converts CO₂ to pure ethanol with a record 2.74% solar‑energy efficiency.
highlights: Record solar‑energy‑to‑ethanol conversion efficiency of 2.74% achieved in lab tests.
MXene‑TiO₂ layer stabilizes Cu₂O, preventing degradation for many hours under illumination.
The system produces only ethanol, eliminating mixed by‑products and simplifying downstream processing.
Photocathode fabricated on FTO substrate using controlled heating to form ultrathin TiO₂ coating.
Research published in Advanced Energy Materials (2026) and led by Pavla Eliášová.

universe_acceleration_analysis_2026.headline: New Study Confirms Cosmic Acceleration, Refutes Recent Slowdown Claim
universe_acceleration_analysis_2026.summary: A fresh analysis of Type Ia supernova data shows the universe’s expansion is still accelerating, overturning a prior study that suggested a deceleration.
highlights: The paper, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, re‑examines host‑galaxy age assumptions.
Lead author Dr Phil Wiseman (University of Southampton) found the earlier Korean analysis mis‑treated galaxy and stellar ages.
Including host‑galaxy mass corrections restores the original evidence for dark‑energy‑driven acceleration.
The work involves Nobel laureates Prof Adam Riess and Prof Brian Schmidt, reinforcing the robustness of supernova cosmology.

galapagos_corals_el_nino_intensity.headline: Modern El Niño Events Outpace Past Millennium, Galápagos Coral Study Shows
galapagos_corals_el_nino_intensity.summary: Coral records from the Galápagos reveal that El Niño events in the last 40 years are stronger than any in the past thousand years, linking intensification to human‑caused warming.
highlights: El Niño intensity in the past 40 years exceeds all recorded events over the previous millennium
Coral oxygen‑isotope and strontium‑to‑calcium ratios provide monthly temperature reconstructions
The 1982–83 and 1997–98 El Niños match the strongest signals in the new coral dataset
Findings, published in Science, align recent ocean thermometer data with long‑term coral evidence

free_falling_atoms_gravity_test.headline: Free‑falling rubidium atoms on Tiangong confirm Galileo’s gravity test to 0.05 thousandths of a percent
free_falling_atoms_gravity_test.summary: Scientists on China’s Tiangong space station observed two clouds of rubidium atoms with different neutron counts falling at virtually identical rates, validating the weak equivalence principle with unprecedented precision.
highlights: Two rubidium atom clouds with differing nuclear masses fell with matching accelerations
The measured agreement reached a precision of 0.05 thousandths of a percent
Results support the equivalence of gravitational and inertial mass, a cornerstone of general relativity

protein_brake_nerve_repair.headline: Blocking AHR Unlocks Nerve Regeneration in Mice After Injury
protein_brake_nerve_repair.summary: Researchers at Icahn School of Medicine found that inhibiting the aryl hydrocarbon receptor enables damaged axons to regrow, improving movement and sensation in mouse models.
highlights: AHR acts as a brake that suppresses axon growth after injury
Pharmacological or genetic AHR inhibition restored axon regeneration in peripheral nerve and spinal cord injury mice
Regeneration was linked to increased protein synthesis and HIF‑1α‑driven repair pathways

plastic_weld_memory_strength.headline: Polyethylene Welds Remember Surface Orientation, Boosting Pipe Joint Strength
plastic_weld_memory_strength.summary: Computer simulations reveal that polyethylene welds retain a molecular memory of their original surfaces, creating extra crystal growth that makes joints stiffer than surrounding pipe material.
highlights: Molecular dynamics simulations modeled millions of polyethylene chains during heating and cooling
Residual surface orientation seeds additional crystallization at the weld line
The reinforced weld pushes failure into the softer surrounding pipe, enhancing overall strength
Effect persists with recycled polyethylene, supporting sustainable pipe construction

natural_hydrogen_generation.headline: Western Australia’s Iron‑Rich Rocks Could Yield Massive Natural Hydrogen
natural_hydrogen_generation.summary: Researchers at Edith Cowan University found that magnetite in Western Australia’s Pilbara formations can naturally produce hydrogen, a process that can be amplified for large‑scale energy use.
highlights: Magnetite releases hydrogen when reacted with hot water at 200 °C under high pressure.
Injecting a solution into banded iron formations increased hydrogen output in laboratory tests.
Rock permeability and fractures control water access, influencing hydrogen generation efficiency.
The study appears in the International Journal of Hydrogen Energy, 2026.

sleep_micro_awakenings_alzheimers_risk.headline: Micro‑Awakenings During Sleep Signal Higher Alzheimer Risk in Middle‑Age Adults
sleep_micro_awakenings_alzheimers_risk.summary: Frequent brief nighttime micro‑awakenings were linked to elevated polygenic Alzheimer risk among healthy adults aged 50‑69, suggesting an early sleep‑based warning sign.
highlights: Study of >500 participants found a correlation between micro‑awakening frequency and Alzheimer polygenic risk in the 50‑69 age
The association was absent in younger adults (18‑31), indicating an age‑dependent effect.
Locus coeruleus integrity, examined with 7‑Tesla MRI, related to REM sleep quality and may underlie the observed link.

low_temp_graphene_growth.headline: Low‑Temperature Graphene Synthesis on Cerium Oxide Enables Sustainable Carbon Recycling
low_temp_graphene_growth.summary: Researchers at Tohoku University and Queen Mary University of London produced graphene and related carbon materials at just 300 °C using acetylene on cerium oxide, opening eco‑friendly recycling pathways.
highlights: Graphene grown at 300 °C on CeO₂ nanoparticles via acetylene CVD
Temperature tuning yields quantum‑dot, aggregated, and porous graphene forms
Acetylene feedstock can be sourced from waste gases, biomass, and recycled plastics

highlights: BDH‑CQ achieved a 30% score on the ARC‑AGI‑1 benchmark, solving three of ten puzzles in two attempts
The model runs on just 150 million parameters, far fewer than Llama 3 70B or Llama 3.1 405B
Token usage is about 11 times lower than GPT 5.6 Luna, dramatically reducing operational expenses

mrna_polya_tail_gastruloids.headline: mRNA deadenylase Cnot8 controls body‑plan patterning in mouse gastruloids
mrna_polya_tail_gastruloids.summary: A single‑cell CRISPR screen shows that loss of Cnot8 elongates poly(A) tails, stabilising transcripts and diverting mesoderm toward ectopic notochord fate.
highlights: Cnot8 loss triggers genome‑wide poly(A) tail elongation and transcript stabilization
Mesodermal cells in Cnot8‑deficient gastruloids adopt ectopic notochord identity
Axial patterning is dramatically altered, linking deadenylation to morphogen signaling

human_d3_receptor_structure.headline: Crystal Structure of Human Dopamine D3 Receptor Reveals Antagonist Binding Details
human_d3_receptor_structure.summary: Scientists have resolved the human dopamine D3 receptor structure at 3.15 Å with the selective antagonist eticlopride, shedding light on ligand interactions.
highlights: Structure solved at 3.15 Å resolution
Eticlopride bound in the orthosteric pocket
Intracellular loop 2 adopts two distinct conformations

airborne_tb_mutation.headline: Drying Airborne TB Bacteria Mutate, Revealing New Drug Target
airborne_tb_mutation.summary: Researchers found that desiccation triggers DNA repair in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, increasing rifampin‑resistance mutations and identifying the Mfd gene as a therapeutic target.
highlights: Desiccation induces oxidative DNA damage in airborne Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
The DNA repair protein Mfd promotes survival and rifampin‑resistance mutations during drying.
Silencing Mfd reduces survival of drug‑resistant TB in aerosol experiments.
Analysis of >50,000 TB genomes shows fewer rifampin‑resistance mutations in strains with Mfd alterations.

diamond_ice_giant.headline: Diamond Melt Experiment Solves Ice Giant Mystery and Boosts Fusion Yield
diamond_ice_giant.summary: LLNL scientists used Omega Laser shocks to melt diamond, confirming its melting point and revealing conditions for diamond rain on Neptune, while suggesting a three‑fold fusion boost.
highlights: Diamond melted at >1 TPa pressures and sun‑like temperatures for a billionth of a second
Measured melting point matches modern quantum‑physics models, resolving a 20‑year discrepancy
Solid diamond is less dense than liquid metallic carbon, enabling diamond rain in ice‑giant interiors
Gentler shock could triple inertial‑confinement‑fusion energy output according to calculations

mass_of_universe_measurement.headline: University of Missouri Team Finds Initial Mass Function Varies Across Star Clusters, Challenging Universal
mass_of_universe_measurement.summary: A new study using Gaia data shows that the stellar initial mass function differs among clusters, implying galaxy mass estimates may need revision.
highlights: Initial mass function (IMF) shows distinct mass ratios in different star clusters
Gaia satellite data of ~2 billion Milky Way stars underpins the analysis
University of Missouri researchers propose environment‑specific IMF models
